Unit 7: Period 7 (1890–1945)

📋 Everything from Unit 7 in one place — the biggest unit, 15 topics from imperialism through WWII. Use the animation to lock in the onset of the Great Depression before your test.
7.1

Contextualizing Period 7

  • Opens with the Spanish-American War (1898), the start of U.S. overseas expansion.
  • Progressive reform → WWI → Great Depression → WWII each expand federal power.
  • By 1945, the U.S. is a global superpower.
Progressive Era
Period 7 at a glance.
7.2

Imperialism: Debates

  • Imperialists: need new markets/resources, duty to “civilize.”
  • Anti-Imperialists (Anti-Imperialist League): colonization contradicts self-government ideals.
Anti-Imperialist League
The imperialism debate.
7.3

The Spanish-American War

  • USS Maine explosion + yellow journalism → war (1898).
  • Treaty of Paris: U.S. gains Puerto Rico, Guam, Philippines.
  • Philippine-American War follows — ironic given anti-colonial justification for the original war.
Yellow journalismTreaty of Paris 1898
The Spanish-American War.
7.4

The Progressives

  • Trust-busting (T. Roosevelt); consumer protection (Pure Food and Drug Act).
  • 17th Amendment: direct election of senators. 19th Amendment (1920): women's suffrage.
Trust-busting19th Amendment
Progressive Era reforms.
7.5

WWI: Military and Diplomacy

  • Unrestricted submarine warfare (Lusitania) → U.S. enters WWI (1917).
  • Wilson's Fourteen Points & League of Nations proposal — Senate refuses to ratify Versailles/join League.
Fourteen PointsLeague of Nations
Trap: The U.S. never joined the League of Nations — a key reason it later failed.
WWI military & diplomacy.
7.6

WWI: Home Front

  • War bonds, propaganda; women & Black Americans fill new jobs.
  • Great Migration of Black Southerners to Northern cities accelerates.
  • Espionage & Sedition Acts criminalize anti-war speech.
Great MigrationEspionage and Sedition Acts
The WWI home front.
7.7

1920s: Innovation in Communication & Tech

  • Ford's mass production makes the automobile affordable; fuels suburbs.
  • Radio creates shared national culture; consumer credit fuels a spending boom.
Mass productionConsumer credit
1920s tech & communication.
7.8

1920s: Cultural & Political Controversies

  • Prohibition (18th Amdt.); Scopes Trial (evolution vs. creationism).
  • Harlem Renaissance; flappers challenge gender norms — traditionalism vs. modernism.
ProhibitionHarlem Renaissance
Traditionalism vs. modernism.
7.9

The Great Depression

  • Overproduction, speculation, wealth inequality → fragile economy.
  • Stock market crash (Oct. 1929) → bank failures → unemployment reaches ~25%.
Stock market crash of 1929
Causes & onset of the Depression.

7.10

The New Deal

  • Three R's: Relief (immediate aid), Recovery (restart growth), Reform (prevent future crises).
  • Social Security: the New Deal's most lasting achievement.
New DealSocial Security
Relief, recovery, reform.
7.11

Interwar Foreign Policy

  • Isolationism & the Neutrality Acts (1935–39).
  • Lend-Lease Act (1941): supplies Britain, a major shift away from neutrality.
  • Pearl Harbor (1941) brings the U.S. fully into WWII.
Neutrality ActsLend-Lease Act
Isolationism to involvement.
7.12

WWII: Mobilization

  • Factories convert to war production; Rosie the Riveter symbolizes women's new roles.
  • Executive Order 9066: forces Japanese American internment — a grave injustice rooted in racial prejudice, not evidence.
Rosie the RiveterExecutive Order 9066
Trap: German & Italian Americans were NOT interned at the same scale — internment targeted Japanese Americans specifically.
WWII home front mobilization.
7.13

WWII: Military

  • Pearl Harbor (1941) → D-Day (June 1944) → Germany surrenders (May 1945).
  • Atomic bombs (Aug. 1945) → Japan surrenders.
D-DayAtomic bomb
Key WWII turning points.
7.14

Postwar Diplomacy

  • Yalta Conference (1945) plans postwar order; the United Nations is founded.
  • Soviet/American visions for Eastern Europe diverge — foreshadows the Cold War.
Yalta ConferenceUnited Nations
Postwar diplomacy & tension.
7.15

Comparison in Period 7

  • 1890: regional/continental power, limited federal economic role.
  • 1945: global superpower, federal government deeply involved in the economy.
Superpower
1890 vs. 1945.

⚠

Commonly Missed on the Exam

  • The U.S. never joined the League of Nations — know this distinguishes it from the later United Nations.
  • Yellow journalism helped cause the Spanish-American War — don't confuse with WWI propaganda.
  • The Great Migration accelerated during WWI due to labor shortages, not after.
  • Executive Order 9066 targeted Japanese Americans specifically — not German or Italian Americans equally.
  • D-Day (June 1944, opens Western front) is not the same as Pearl Harbor (Dec. 1941, brings the U.S. into the war) — know the order.
  • Distinguish Neutrality Acts (isolationist) from Lend-Lease (interventionist) — opposite directions in U.S. policy.
